# Homework 11: Prediction with Many Regressors

## Grading rubric

Grading Rubric (per question):
2 points if complete and correct
0 points otherwise

## Retrieving your work

This and all future homework `.Rmd` files are written in Markdown. The `.Rmd` file can be rendered as an `.html` file for easier viewing.

Once you have opened the `.Rmd` file, you may begin writing your answers beneath each problem. Do not remove any of the original problems from the file, because that makes it more difficult for me to grade your assignment.

## Submitting your work

When you upload your files to Canvas, submit two files:

1. Your reproducible document file (`.Rmd`), saved as `homework11-ID.Rmd`. For example, `homework11-jperrigan.Rmd`.
2. Your rendered reproducible document file (`.html`), saved as `homework11-ID.html`. For example, `homework11-jperrigan.html`.

Your ID is your Canvas username. It is also the text before the `@` symbol in your UNO email address. You may submit more than once; only the latest submission before the deadline will be graded. Before submitting, make sure your `.Rmd` renders to `.html`.

All students are expected to complete all problems. The data for this assignment are simulated in this file, so no local data files are needed. You'll want to use the sample notebook and Chapter 14 of Stock and Watson to answer the questions.

## Data and setup

Suppose a college wants to predict students' end-of-semester scores out of 100. The simulated data below contain 400 students and 15 possible predictors. 

Only `study_hours` and `attendance` are used to generate final scores in this simulation. The other variables are included to show what can happen when a model uses a lot of predictors.

The data are divided into an estimation sample and a test sample. Use the estimation sample to fit models. Use the test sample to check how well the predictions perform on observations that weren't used to estimate the models. 

The outcome and all score prediction errors are measured in final points.

```{r}
set.seed(3300)

# number of students
n <- 400
# number of predictors
p <- 15


# generating a vector of random numbers from the normal distribution of length n
common_factor <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# the predictors share a common component (coming from the same student), so some are correlated.

# this code is creating a matrix called X, with n rows and p columns
# it starts by taking the vector of random numbers and creating a matrix where the first row is the first element in the vector across all p columns, the second row is the second element in the vector across all p columns, etc.
# then it multiplies all of those elements by sqrt(0.25)
X <- sqrt(0.25) * matrix(common_factor, nrow = n, ncol = p) +
  
  # now it's generating a new vector of length n * p and arranging them into a matrix with n rows and p columns, and multiplying that by the sqrt(0.75)
  
  # then adding the two matrices together
  sqrt(0.75) * matrix(rnorm(n * p, mean = 0, sd = 1), nrow = n, ncol = p)

# now renaming the column with "x" plus the number of the parameter
colnames(X) <- paste0("x", seq_len(p))


X[, "x1"] <- exp(log(8) + 0.25 * X[, "x1"])  # positive study hours, centered near 8

# qlogis is the quantile function for the logistic distribution, it gives the log odds for a probability of 0.85 here
# plogis converts log odds into a probability so keeps x2 between 0 and 1
X[, "x2"] <- plogis(qlogis(0.85) + 0.35 * X[, "x2"])  # attendance proportion
```

```{r}
# now we'll create the student data by using X
student_data <- as_tibble(X) %>%
  mutate(
    study_hours = x1,
    attendance = x2,
    course_score = 75 + 2 * (study_hours-8) + 10 * (attendance-0.85) + rnorm(n, sd = 8),
    student = seq_len(n)
  ) %>%
  select(student, course_score, study_hours, attendance, starts_with("x"))

# randomly assign 70% of observations to estimation and the rest to testing.
estimation_rows <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.70 * n))
estimation_data <- student_data[estimation_rows, ]
test_data <- student_data[-estimation_rows, ]

# a small model uses two predictors, the larger model uses all 15 x variables.
small_model <- lm(course_score ~ study_hours + attendance, data = estimation_data)
large_model <- lm(course_score ~ ., data = estimation_data %>% select(course_score, starts_with("x")))

# make predictions for the held-out test sample.
small_predictions <- predict(small_model, newdata = test_data)
large_predictions <- predict(
  large_model,
  newdata = test_data %>% select(starts_with("x"))
)

```
